title: LCK_M LOW_PRIORITY and ABORT_BLOCKERS Wait Types in SQL Server
verdict: Time in a _LOW_PRIORITY wait is the feature working: the operation waits for its long-term intent shared lock, or the final schema modification lock, at low priority until MAX_DURATION expires, without blocking other sessions the way a...
what_to_do: Use WAIT_AT_LOW_PRIORITY on online rebuilds and partition switches on busy systems; it is the polite way to run them. Choose ABORT_AFTER_WAIT on purpose: NONE carries on waiting normally, SELF gives up, BLOCKERS kills what is in the way. The ALTER INDEX documentation has the full syntax. If the low-priority window keeps running out, find the long sessions holding the table and schedule around them.

title: AM_INDBUILD_ALLOCATION and AM_SCHEMAMGR_UNSHARED_CACHE Wait Types in SQL Server
verdict: No. Neither is a known contention point.

title: ASSEMBLY_LOAD and CLR Assembly Wait Types in SQL Server
verdict: Rarely. None of them is a known contention point.

title: ASYNC_DISKPOOL_LOCK Wait Type in SQL Server
verdict: Not as contention. It is not a known bottleneck, and it was zero on our SQL Server 2025 lab.

title: ASYNC_IO_COMPLETION Wait Type in SQL Server
verdict: It is expected in volume during backup and maintenance windows.
what_to_do: If it maps onto backup and maintenance windows, judge those jobs by duration rather than by the wait total. Move heavy maintenance away from peak hours, and use backup compression, which writes fewer bytes at the cost of CPU. If checkpoint bursts are the driver, indirect checkpoints ( TARGET_RECOVERY_TIME, the default for new databases from SQL Server 2016) spread writes more evenly. If the data files show high read or write stalls outside backup windows, that is a storage conversation, with the per-file numbers as evidence.

title: ASYNC_NETWORK_IO Wait Type in SQL Server
verdict: Very common and almost always harmless.
when_to_ignore: SSMS result grid, SSMS displays results incrementally as they arrive.
what_to_do: If queries return too many rows: Add WHERE clauses to filter earlier Add TOP or pagination (OFFSET/FETCH) to return only what's needed Move aggregation into SQL (GROUP BY, SUM, COUNT) rather than returning raw rows to the application If it's cursor-style row-by-row processing: Refactor the application to process results in batches Read the whole result set first, then do the slow work (writing files, calling APIs), instead of doing it between reads Can the processing move into SQL Server (stored procedure, table-valued function)? If it's a reporting tool pulling large data sets: Review whether the report actually needs all those rows Consider pre-aggregating into summary tables for common report patterns If network latency is genuinely high: Move application closer to SQL Server (same data centre) Check network infrastructure, QoS, routing, VPN encryption overhead Consider reducing the size of result sets to minimise round trips

title: BACKUP Wait Type in SQL Server
verdict: Not in itself. It is not a known contention point, and it was zero on our SQL Server 2025 lab.

title: BACKUPIO and BACKUPBUFFER Wait Types in SQL Server
verdict: Yes, during backup windows.
what_to_do: Enable backup compression, the single highest-impact change you can make to improve backup performance: -- For a single backup: BACKUP DATABASE [YourDatabase] TO DISK = 'D:\Backups\YourDatabase.bak' WITH COMPRESSION, STATS = 10; -- Set as default for all future backups: EXEC sp_configure 'backup compression default', 1; RECONFIGURE; Fewer bytes means less write I/O and less network transfer, at the cost of CPU while the backup runs. How much it saves depends on the data: read compression_pct in the history query after the first compressed backup. Stripe across multiple backup files, write to multiple destinations simultaneously: BACKUP DATABASE [YourDatabase] TO DISK = '\\backup1\share\YourDatabase_1.bak', DISK = '\\backup2\share\YourDatabase_2.bak', DISK = 'D:\LocalBackup\YourDatabase_3.bak' WITH COMPRESSION, STATS = 5; This spreads I/O across destinations and can multiply effective throughput. Move backups to faster or dedicated backup storage, a dedicated backup LUN or a local fast disk for landing backups, followed by a secondary copy job, is faster than writing directly to a shared NAS over the network. Tune BUFFERCOUNT and MAXTRANSFERSIZE, for large databases, increasing these can improve backup throughput: BACKUP DATABASE [YourDatabase] TO DISK = 'D:\Backups\YourDatabase.bak' WITH COMPRESSION, MAXTRANSFERSIZE = 4194304, BUFFERCOUNT = 50; MAXTRANSFERSIZE = 4194304 (4 MB) is the maximum. [trimmed for size - the full steps are in the write-up linked below]

title: BACKUPTHREAD Wait Type in SQL Server
verdict: Not by itself. Microsoft says wait times might be long, from several minutes to several hours, and that if the task being waited on is doing I/O, this wait does not indicate a problem.

title: BAD_PAGE_PROCESS Wait Type in SQL Server
verdict: Any presence is a corruption signal, not a performance discussion.
what_to_do: Run DBCC CHECKDB on the affected databases to see how far the damage goes; DBCC CHECKDB Found Corruption walks through reading the output. Restore from backups where you can: page restore for a few isolated pages, a full restore for wider damage. Do not reach for REPAIR_ALLOW_DATA_LOSS before restore options are exhausted. Bring in the storage team at the same time; corruption that keeps coming back will not stop until its cause does.

title: BPSORT Wait Type in SQL Server

title: CHECK_TABLES_INITIALIZATION Wait Type in SQL Server

title: CHECK_TABLES_THREAD_BARRIER Wait Type in SQL Server

title: CLR_MANUAL_EVENT Wait Type in SQL Server

title: CLR_SEMAPHORE Wait Type in SQL Server

title: CMEMPARTITIONED Wait Type in SQL Server
verdict: Rarely. It is not described in any detail anywhere, and it was zero on our SQL Server 2025 lab.

title: CMEMTHREAD Wait Type in SQL Server
verdict: A little is normal on busy systems.
what_to_do: If the hot object relates to compilation, reduce ad hoc churn: parameterise the common patterns so plans are reused. Check the build. There have been several CMEMTHREAD fixes over the years, so patch before tuning. On SQL Server 2012 and earlier, trace flag 8048 moved NUMA-partitioned objects to per-CPU partitions. From SQL Server 2014 SP2 and 2016 this is dynamic and handled by the engine, so the flag is not needed on current versions. Re-measure after each change, comparing wait share over intervals rather than one snapshot.

title: COLUMNSTORE_BUILD_THROTTLE Wait Type in SQL Server
verdict: Some of it is a fixed cost at the start of every parallel columnstore build.

title: COMMIT_TABLE Wait Type in SQL Server
verdict: It can be, though nothing documents it.

title: CXPACKET and CXCONSUMER Wait Types in SQL Server
verdict: Yes, they will appear on any server that runs parallel queries.
when_to_ignore: Analytics and reporting workloads, parallel queries are beneficial for large aggregations, sorts, and scans.
what_to_do: In priority order. Start with the query: the settings in steps 3 and 4 are instance-wide, so they change every query on the server, and they need evidence that many queries show the same pattern. STEP 1

title: CXROWSET_SYNC Wait Type in SQL Server
verdict: No. It is not a known contention point, and our SQL Server 2025 lab had about 200 waits totalling a quarter of a second in a day.

title: CXSYNC_CONSUMER Wait Type in SQL Server
verdict: Read it the way you read CXPACKET: it shows parallel plans are running, which is often what you want.

title: CXSYNC_PORT Wait Type in SQL Server
verdict: Treat it as part of the CX family: evidence of parallelism, not proof of trouble, and not a reason on its own to cut MAXDOP.
what_to_do: Reduce what the blocking operator has to process: an index that provides the order, tighter predicates, or fresh statistics for accurate memory grants. Keep parallelism settings deliberate. A cost threshold for parallelism raised from the default of 5 keeps cheap queries serial; MAXDOP and cost threshold has the reasoning. Change MAXDOP only as a considered setting for the workload, not as a reaction to this wait existing.

title: DAC_INIT Wait Type in SQL Server
verdict: No. It is a one-off at startup; our SQL Server 2025 lab had a single wait of about a second.

title: EC Wait Type in SQL Server

verdict: Not in practice. It is not a known contention point; our SQL Server 2025 lab had about 750 waits totalling under a fifth of a second.

title: EXECSYNC Wait Type in SQL Server

title: FCB_REPLICA_READ and FCB_REPLICA_WRITE Wait Types in SQL Server
verdict: Not as contention. Neither is a known bottleneck; our SQL Server 2025 lab had four FCB_REPLICA_WRITE waits in a day, all under a millisecond.

title: FFT_NSO_DB_LIST and FFT_RECOVERY Wait Types in SQL Server
verdict: No. FFT_NSO_DB_LIST is not a known contention point, and both were zero on our SQL Server 2025 lab.

title: FGCB_ADD_REMOVE Wait Type in SQL Server
verdict: Yes, when it shows real time, because while one session grows a file, others that need that filegroup's file information queue behind it.
what_to_do: Pre-size data and log files for their expected size plus headroom, so autogrowth is a backstop rather than routine. Turn on instant file initialization for data files. Use fixed growth sizes, not percentages, and keep log growths moderate; on SQL Server 2022 and later, log growths of 64 MB or less can skip zeroing. Size tempdb for its normal peak; it is recreated at its configured size on every restart.

title: FT_IFTSHC_MUTEX and FT_IFTS_RWLOCK Wait Types in SQL Server
verdict: No. Neither is reported as a contention point; both were zero on our SQL Server 2025 lab.

title: FT_IFTS_SCHEDULER_IDLE_WAIT Wait Type in SQL Server
verdict: No. It can be safely ignored, and Get Wait Statistics filters it out by default.

title: FT_MASTER_MERGE Wait Type in SQL Server
verdict: Not as contention. It follows master merges, which you schedule, and it is not a known contention point.

title: HADR_AG_MUTEX Wait Type in SQL Server
verdict: Rarely. It is not a known contention point, because Availability Group configuration changes are infrequent.

title: HADR_ARCONTROLLER and HADR_FILESTREAM_IOMGR Wait Types in SQL Server
verdict: No. Neither is a known contention point.

title: HADR_CLUSAPI_CALL Wait Type in SQL Server
verdict: Normally no. It is commonly filtered as benign, and Get Wait Statistics filters it out by default.

title: HADR_DATABASE_FLOW_CONTROL Wait Type in SQL Server
verdict: Small amounts on a busy AG are the gate doing its job.
what_to_do: Compare the log generation rate on the primary with what the link carries. If generation is higher, reduce log volume, for example by trimming index maintenance and batching loads, or improve the link. Check the secondary: log disk latency and redo queue. Know the version. SQL Server 2022 raised the number of messages each gate allows; on SQL Server 2019 CU9, 2017 CU18 and 2016 SP1 CU16 and later, trace flag 12310 at startup gives the higher limits, and it cannot be set with DBCC TRACEON. Test before using it.

title: HADR_FILESTREAM_IOMGR_IOCOMPLETION Wait Type in SQL Server
verdict: No. It is a timer, commonly filtered as benign, and Get Wait Statistics filters it out by default.

title: HADR_GROUP_COMMIT Wait Type in SQL Server
verdict: By design, no. Microsoft calls it an expected condition that optimizes the log I/O, capture, and send operations.

title: HADR_LOGCAPTURE_WAIT Wait Type in SQL Server
verdict: No. Microsoft calls it an expected wait if the log scan is caught up to the end of log or is reading from disk, and Get Wait Statistics filters it out by default.

title: HADR_LOGPROGRESS_SYNC Wait Type in SQL Server
verdict: Small amounts come with any synchronous AG.
what_to_do: Check the build against known fixes for this pattern, starting with the one above. Resolve scheduler problems on the primary, such as non-yielding threads or CPU saturation. Re-measure HADR_SYNC_COMMIT alongside this wait after each change.

title: HADR_NOTIFICATION_DEQUEUE Wait Type in SQL Server
verdict: No. It is commonly filtered as benign, and Get Wait Statistics filters it out by default.

title: HADR_SEEDING_LIMIT_BACKUPS Wait Type in SQL Server
verdict: It appears not. It is documented as internal use only, from SQL Server 2016, and the only description is anecdotal: long waits, thousands of seconds, for the length of some automatic seeding operations, and a wait that seems benign.

title: HADR_SYNC_COMMIT Wait Type in SQL Server
verdict: Some HADR_SYNC_COMMIT is the inherent cost of synchronous replication.
what_to_do: If it's a network latency problem: Co-locate synchronous secondaries, same data centre, same network segment, same rack if possible For secondaries that must be remote (DR in a different city): evaluate whether asynchronous commit is acceptable for that replica. Asynchronous commit eliminates HADR_SYNC_COMMIT for that replica entirely, at the cost of potential data loss on failover (RPO > 0). You can have one synchronous secondary local and one asynchronous secondary remote. If it's a slow secondary log disk: Move the secondary log file to faster storage, ideally matching the primary's storage tier Ensure the secondary log disk isn't shared with other high-I/O workloads If the secondary is a readable secondary under load: Review the read workload going to the secondary, heavy reporting queries during peak hours can degrade secondary I/O and redo performance Consider Resource Governor on the secondary to limit read workload resource consumption Schedule heavy reports for off-peak hours If it's commit frequency: Batch transactions where the application allows, reduce the number of individual commits Review application code for row-by-row commit loops

title: HADR_TIMER_TASK Wait Type in SQL Server
verdict: No. HADR_TIMER_TASK is Availability Group timer bookkeeping, and most of its total is time spent waiting for the next run of a scheduled task.

title: HADR_TRANSPORT_FLOW_CONTROL Wait Type in SQL Server
verdict: Short bursts on a busy Availability Group are the gate doing its job, and the gates do not change the synchronization health of a replica.
what_to_do: Check the link to the replica the check named: latency with ping, and the Resent Messages/sec counter. The fix is more network bandwidth, or removing or reducing other traffic on the link. Check the secondary's log disk. If the log file shares a disk with the data files and a reporting workload, move it to its own disk so hardening, and the acknowledgement, are not queued behind reads. Reduce the bursts. Index rebuilds and bulk loads across several databases on the same replica all count against the one transport gate, so spread them out rather than running them together. Know the version. SQL Server 2022 raised the number of messages each gate allows; on SQL Server 2019 CU9, 2017 CU18 and 2016 SP1 CU16 and later, trace flag 12310 at startup gives the higher limits, and it cannot be set with DBCC TRACEON. A higher limit lets more messages be outstanding; it does not make a slow link faster. Test before using it.

title: HADR_WORK_POOL Wait Type in SQL Server
verdict: No. HADR_WORK_POOL is concurrency control inside the Availability Group background worker pool, and it is not reported as a contention point.

title: HADR_WORK_QUEUE Wait Type in SQL Server
verdict: No. Microsoft calls it an expected wait when there are ready workers waiting for new work, which it describes as the normal state.

title: HP_SPOOL_BARRIER Wait Type in SQL Server
verdict: If you can see it at all, the useful conclusion is about your build.

verdict: Usually not on its own; steady amounts on an analytics workload are the cost of batch mode.

verdict: Usually not on its own; steady amounts on an analytics workload are the cost of batch mode.

title: HTREPARTITION Wait Type in SQL Server
verdict: Usually not on its own; steady amounts on an analytics workload are the cost of batch mode.

title: IMPPROV_IOWAIT Wait Type in SQL Server
verdict: Only as much as your bulk loads need to be fast.

title: IO_COMPLETION Wait Type in SQL Server
verdict: During backup windows, not from the backup itself, because its I/O is counted as BACKUPIO and ASYNC_IO_COMPLETION.
what_to_do: For sort spills (the most common cause): The root cause is almost always a missing index or stale statistics. A query that spills to disk is doing work it should not need to do. Identify the spilling queries from dm_exec_query_stats above Run their execution plans in SSMS with "Include Actual Execution Plan", look for Sort operators with a yellow warning triangle ("Warnings: Operator used tempdb to spill data") Check for missing indexes on the tables involved: Get Missing Indexes lists the candidates the optimiser already wanted, with example output and what each column means. Copy the T-SQL from that page and run it in SSMS, or run the Get-MissingIndexes wrapper from a clone of dba-tools. Update statistics on the involved tables If the query legitimately needs to sort large data sets (e.g. a reporting query), consider whether the result set can be reduced before sorting For tempdb I/O performance in general: Tempdb data files should be on fast storage, ideally the same SSD/NVMe tier as production data Multiple tempdb data files (one per logical processor, up to 8) reduce allocation contention, though they do not directly improve sort spill I/O For DBCC-driven IO_COMPLETION: Run DBCC CHECKDB during off-peak hours DBCC CHECKDB with PHYSICAL_ONLY is faster and generates less tempdb I/O (though it checks less)

title: IO_QUEUE_LIMIT Wait Type in SQL Server
verdict: If it is sustained, it is a throughput ceiling, and what matters is where the ceiling comes from.
what_to_do: Reduce the I/O first: missing indexes turn seeks into scans, and scans drive I/O. That is cheaper than a bigger tier. Move I/O-heavy maintenance, such as rebuilds and integrity checks, away from the busiest hours. If the workload is already lean, scale the tier, or on SQL Server the storage, to match real demand.

title: KSOURCE_WAKEUP Wait Type in SQL Server
verdict: No. Microsoft says long waits are expected and don't indicate a problem.

title: LATCH_DT Wait Type in SQL Server
verdict: Almost never. LATCH_DT should be one of the smallest numbers in your wait profile, if it appears at all; it was zero on our SQL Server 2025 lab.

title: LATCH_EX Wait Type in SQL Server
verdict: A small amount is normal.

title: LATCH_KP Wait Type in SQL Server
verdict: Practically never. A LATCH_KP wait means a thread wanted to pin a structure while another thread held it for destruction, which is a narrow window, so expect zero or close to it; it was zero on our SQL Server 2025 lab.

title: LATCH_NL Wait Type in SQL Server
verdict: No, and you should never see it with a non-zero value; it was zero on our SQL Server 2025 lab.

title: LATCH_SH Wait Type in SQL Server
verdict: Low values are normal.
what_to_do: Match the top class to its row in the LATCH_EX class table, which has the documented causes and fixes: ACCESS_METHODS_DATASET_PARENT for parallel scans, ACCESS_METHODS_HOBT_VIRTUAL_ROOT for root splits, the allocation cache classes for concurrent inserts, FGCB_ADD_REMOVE for file growth. For a parallel scan class, review MAXDOP and cost threshold and index the queries driving the scans. If the class is documented as internal use only and it dominates for long, a support case is the honest next step.

title: LATCH_UP Wait Type in SQL Server
verdict: Rarely on its own; our SQL Server 2025 lab had 9 waits totalling 2 ms.

title: LAZYWRITER_SLEEP Wait Type in SQL Server
verdict: No. Microsoft says don't consider this state when you're looking for user stalls, and Get Wait Statistics filters it out by default.

title: LCK_M_IS Wait Type in SQL Server
verdict: Sustained time is worth a look, because readers are queuing behind whole-table locks.
what_to_do: Break large modifications into batches that stay under the escalation threshold, or schedule them away from read-heavy periods. Remove table-lock hints that are not needed. If readers must coexist with heavy writes, consider READ_COMMITTED_SNAPSHOT: readers then use row versions instead of shared locks. Writers still block writers.

title: LCK_M_IX Wait Type in SQL Server
verdict: Yes, if it is sustained, because modifications are held up at table level and users notice.
what_to_do: If a reporting query with table hints is blocking writers, remove the hint, or move the report to a readable secondary or to snapshot isolation. Batch large modifications to stay under the escalation threshold, and keep transactions short. If an application runs serializable without meaning to, set the isolation level explicitly in its code or connection.

title: LCK_M_RIn_NL Wait Type in SQL Server
verdict: It matters for the same reason as the other range lock waits: most systems never chose serializable on purpose.

title: LCK_M_RS_S Wait Type in SQL Server
verdict: Range lock waits deserve attention because most workloads never intend serializable isolation, and range locks block a much wider surface than row locks, so blocking and deadlocks climb once they appear.
what_to_do: If serializable is unintended, fix the source: the framework setting, the hint, or the connection. If it is required, index the predicate columns so the range locks stay narrow, and keep those transactions short. Set the isolation level explicitly at the start of each unit of work, rather than relying on whatever the connection was left with.

title: LCK_M_RS_U Wait Type in SQL Server
verdict: Treat it as two questions: is serializable intentional, and is the range being locked narrow?

title: LCK_M_RX_X Wait Type in SQL Server
verdict: Yes, when it shows real time, because range locks cover more than the rows being changed, so serializable writers block each other more than you would expect.
what_to_do: Find out why the transaction is serializable. If it is a framework default rather than a design choice, set the isolation level explicitly in the application. Rework upserts. Under READ COMMITTED, an INSERT... WHERE NOT EXISTS backed by a unique constraint, with a retry on a duplicate key error, avoids range locks entirely. Index the key you search on. A seek locks a narrow range; a scan under serializable locks everything it reads. If serializable is truly needed, serialise the writers on purpose, for example with sp_getapplock, so they queue instead of deadlocking.

title: LCK_M_SCH_M Wait Type in SQL Server
verdict: Yes, while it lasts, because it hurts twice.
what_to_do: Kill or complete the blocker if it is an abandoned transaction; DBCC OPENTRAN in the database points at the oldest one, and killing the session rolls its open work back, which can take a while on a big transaction. Schedule DDL for quiet windows, and use ONLINE = ON where the edition allows. An online rebuild still takes a short shared lock at the start and a brief SCH-M at the end, so it can still queue behind a long transaction, but it does not hold the table for the whole rebuild. On SQL Server 2014 and later, use WAIT_AT_LOW_PRIORITY with ABORT_AFTER_WAIT so index operations and partition switches give up or remove blockers deliberately, instead of freezing the table for everyone. Those waits show as the LOW_PRIORITY and ABORT_BLOCKERS variants. Keep ETL steps that switch partitions or truncate tables away from long reports on the same tables, since both take SCH-M.

title: LCK_M_SCH_S Wait Type in SQL Server
verdict: Yes, and it is dramatic when it happens.
what_to_do: Clear the head of the chain: let the long query finish, or kill the session if it is an abandoned transaction. Killing a session rolls its work back, which can take a while. If the DDL itself has to give way, cancel it; the queued queries continue as soon as its request is gone. Move DDL to quiet windows, and use ONLINE = ON where the edition allows. An online rebuild still needs a short lock at the start and a brief Sch-M at the end, but it does not hold the table for the whole rebuild. On SQL Server 2014 and later, use WAIT_AT_LOW_PRIORITY on index rebuilds and partition switches so the DDL waits without blocking everyone else. Those waits show up as the LOW_PRIORITY and ABORT_BLOCKERS variants.

title: LCK_M_SIX Wait Type in SQL Server
verdict: It is one of the rarer lock waits, so a meaningful amount stands out.
what_to_do: Look at the waiting transaction first. If it reads with TABLOCK or HOLDLOCK and then updates, drop the hint or split the read from the write. If it runs under REPEATABLE READ or SERIALIZABLE, check whether that isolation level is needed; under READ COMMITTED an ordinary update takes intent exclusive locks, not SIX. Reduce escalation: index the predicate so the transaction touches fewer rows, or work in smaller batches. Run competing copies of the same job one after another, or split them by key range.

title: LCK_M_X, LCK_M_S, and LCK_M_U Wait Types in SQL Server
verdict: Small amounts of locking are inherent in transactional systems.
when_to_ignore: Short, infrequent lock waits, a small amount of LCK_M_X from occasional row-level conflicts is normal.
what_to_do: In order. The first step is diagnosis and the rest are fixes, narrowing from the transaction down to the pattern behind it. STEP 1

title: LOGBUFFER Wait Type in SQL Server
verdict: Some is normal on write-heavy systems.
what_to_do: Put the log on dedicated low-latency storage; log writes are sequential and latency-sensitive. Reduce log volume where the design allows: batch small commits, avoid needless index churn, and use minimally logged operations for bulk work. Where the business accepts a small window of possible data loss, delayed durability removes the commit-time flush wait; understand the trade before using it.

title: LOGMGR Wait Type in SQL Server
verdict: Almost never in a normal wait profile, because databases do not usually close while the instance is running; it was zero on our SQL Server 2025 lab.

title: LOGMGR_FLUSH Wait Type in SQL Server

title: LOGMGR_QUEUE Wait Type in SQL Server

title: LOGMGR_RESERVE_APPEND Wait Type in SQL Server
verdict: Yes, whenever it shows up, though it is unusual to see at all; it was zero on our SQL Server 2025 lab.
what_to_do: Clear whatever log_reuse_wait_desc names: take the log backup, finish or kill the long transaction, or fix the replica or replication that is behind. Give the log room: a fixed growth increment the drive can actually hold, and enough free space on the drive. Pre-size the log for your largest normal burst plus headroom, so growth is the exception. In full recovery, check log backups run often enough for the amount of change.

title: LOGPOOL Wait Types in SQL Server
verdict: No. They are not known contention points, and they stay small next to the real log waits.

title: MEMORY_ALLOCATION_EXT Wait Type in SQL Server
verdict: Almost never. Get Wait Statistics filters it out by default, and its source notes it as millions of microsecond waits on every instance.

title: METADATA_LAZYCACHE_RWLOCK Wait Type in SQL Server
verdict: Not on any current version, because it does not exist there.

title: MSQL_DQ Wait Type in SQL Server
verdict: It is honest accounting of remote time, so it matters as much as your workload depends on distributed queries.

title: MSQL_XP Wait Type in SQL Server
verdict: The wait is honest accounting; the question is what it measures.
what_to_do: Find the procedure and the caller from the check, and time the external work it does; a hanging procedure usually traces back to a hanging dependency. Replace legacy XP use where you can: SQL Agent job steps, PowerShell or application-side services cover most of what they were used for, without loading foreign DLLs into SQL Server. For a vendor's procedure, give the vendor the wait times and the calling statement; the fix is in their code.

title: OLEDB Wait Type in SQL Server
verdict: Check the shape before anything else.
what_to_do: If it lines up with integrity checks or a monitoring tool, it is part of your baseline. Check the tool's polling interval if it seems excessive. For linked server time, push filters and aggregation to the remote side, for example with OPENQUERY and the full filtered query, so less data crosses the link. Stage remote data locally for recurring reports, and take slowness on the remote side to the team that owns that server.

title: ONDEMAND_TASK_QUEUE Wait Type in SQL Server
verdict: No. Microsoft says long wait times indicate that there have been no high priority requests to process, and shouldn't cause concern, and Get Wait Statistics filters it out by default.

title: PAGEIOLATCH_DT Wait Type in SQL Server
verdict: Practically never; expect zero or close to it.

title: PAGEIOLATCH_EX Wait Type in SQL Server
verdict: Some is normal on any server that changes data, because not every page a write touches will be cached.
what_to_do: Index the predicate of large updates and deletes. Fewer pages read means fewer waits, and it is the fix that removes the reads rather than speeding them up. Move big changes to cold data off-peak. Archive jobs, purges and backfills read old pages by design. Run them when they are not competing with production reads, and in batches so each one finishes quickly. Give the buffer pool enough memory. If pages are being evicted and read back, more memory for SQL Server keeps the changing data cached. Leave the operating system room to work. Use sequential keys for insert-heavy tables. IDENTITY, a SEQUENCE or NEWSEQUENTIALID() keeps inserts on the last page, which stays in memory. A fill factor below 100 trades space for fewer splits where the key cannot change. Faster storage for the data files. If reads are slow at the file level, moving data files to SSD or NVMe shortens every one of these waits. Two write-side fixes often suggested for this wait help a different one. File growth without instant file initialisation waits on PREEMPTIVE_OS_WRITEFILEGATHER while the new space is zeroed, and checkpoint tuning changes write bursts, which this wait does not measure.

title: PAGEIOLATCH_KP Wait Type in SQL Server
verdict: Practically never; expect zero or close to it.

title: PAGEIOLATCH_NL Wait Type in SQL Server
verdict: No, and a non-zero value would itself be odd; it was zero on our SQL Server 2025 lab.

title: PAGEIOLATCH_SH Wait Type in SQL Server
verdict: Some PAGEIOLATCH_SH is normal.
when_to_ignore: After a restart. The buffer pool starts empty, so the first read of each page comes from disk until the working set is cached again.
what_to_do: Which fix applies depends entirely on what the diagnosis above returned. These are not steps to work through in order; pick the row that matches your evidence. What the diagnosis says What to do Storage latency is high avg_read_ms consistently above about 15 ms Move the data files to faster storage. Check whether the array is shared and already busy, and confirm the latency outside SQL Server with Performance Monitor’s PhysicalDisk\Avg. Disk sec/Read for that volume. Fix the volume before touching the instance. Latency is fine but reads are constant low avg_read_ms, high read counts This is buffer pool churn. Check whether max server memory has been set too low, look for other processes eating RAM on the box, and add indexes to cut the logical reads of the worst queries. Add RAM only once the working set genuinely does not fit. One query is responsible Add the missing index, validating it against an execution plan first. Consider partitioning if the query only needs a slice of the table, and check whether it needs every row it asks for or can filter earlier.

title: PAGEIOLATCH_UP Wait Type in SQL Server
verdict: Judge it by average wait time, like the rest of the family.
what_to_do: If per-file read latency is high, this is a storage problem, not an allocation one; take the per-file numbers to the storage team. Check memory: page life expectancy and max server memory, since eviction pressure sends more reads to disk. If it clusters in tempdb alongside PAGELATCH_UP, treat it as part of tempdb allocation contention and follow the tempdb file guidance on PAGELATCH_EX.

title: PAGELATCH_DT Wait Type in SQL Server
verdict: Practically never. Expect zero or close to it; it was zero on our SQL Server 2025 lab.

title: PAGELATCH_EX Wait Type in SQL Server
verdict: A little is normal on any busy server, latches are how SQL Server protects pages in memory, and short waits are just the system working.
when_to_ignore: Low levels alongside other waits, if PAGELATCH_EX is a few percent of total waits and nothing points at tempdb allocation pages, it's just normal latch coordination.
what_to_do: Add tempdb data files, equally sized. The long-standing guidance: one data file per logical core up to 8, then add more (in fours) only if contention persists. All files the same size with the same autogrowth so proportional fill stays balanced. -- Example: add a second, equally-sized tempdb data file ALTER DATABASE tempdb ADD FILE ( NAME = tempdev2, FILENAME = 'T:\tempdb\tempdev2.ndf', SIZE = 1024MB, FILEGROWTH = 256MB ); Keep the files uniform. On SQL Server 2016 and later, uniform autogrowth across tempdb files is the default behaviour. On older versions enable trace flags 1117 (grow all files together) and 1118 (uniform extents) to get the same effect. Use memory-optimized tempdb metadata (SQL Server 2019+). If the contention is on system-table metadata rather than allocation pages, this removes it: ALTER SERVER CONFIGURATION SET MEMORY_OPTIMIZED TEMPDB_METADATA = ON; -- requires a restart to take effect Fix last-page insert contention (user databases). When the hot page is in a user database, adding tempdb files won't help. On SQL Server 2019+ use OPTIMIZE_FOR_SEQUENTIAL_KEY on the offending index; on older versions consider a non-sequential key (e.g. a hash or reversed key) to spread inserts across pages. ALTER INDEX PK_Orders ON dbo.Orders SET (OPTIMIZE_FOR_SEQUENTIAL_KEY = ON); The word to remember is memory: PAGELATCH is threads queuing on a hot in-memory page, and nine times out of ten that page lives in tempdb.

title: PAGELATCH_KP Wait Type in SQL Server
verdict: No; expect it at or near zero.

title: PAGELATCH_NL Wait Type in SQL Server
verdict: No, and you should never see it accumulate; it was zero on our SQL Server 2025 lab.

title: PAGELATCH_SH Wait Type in SQL Server
verdict: A small amount is normal on any busy system.
what_to_do: For tempdb, follow the tempdb guidance: several equally sized data files, as many as logical processors up to eight to start with, adding more in fours if contention continues. For last-page insert contention on SQL Server 2019 and later, consider OPTIMIZE_FOR_SEQUENTIAL_KEY = ON on the index, or a key that does not always land on the last page. For a hot lookup page, reduce how often it changes while it is being read, or cache it in the application.

title: PAGELATCH_UP Wait Type in SQL Server
verdict: Yes, when it is sustained, because many sessions are queuing to update the same allocation page.
what_to_do: Follow the tempdb guidance: several equally sized data files, as many as logical processors up to eight to start with, adding more in fours if contention continues, all growing by the same amount. Know what your version already does. SQL Server 2016 made the old trace flag 1117 and 1118 behaviour the default for tempdb; SQL Server 2019 added concurrent PFS updates and optional memory-optimized tempdb metadata; SQL Server 2022 added concurrent GAM and SGAM updates. Reduce tempdb churn at the source: fewer throwaway temp objects, and temp table caching in frequently called procedures.

title: PARALLEL_BACKUP_QUEUE Wait Type in SQL Server
verdict: No. It is bounded by how often you read backup metadata, and it was zero on our SQL Server 2025 lab.

title: PARALLEL_REDO_DRAIN_WORKER Wait Type in SQL Server
verdict: No. The secondary replica redo model write-up lists it among the waits without performance impact and says to expect it regularly.

title: PARALLEL_REDO_FLOW_CONTROL Wait Type in SQL Server
verdict: It can be. When it occurs frequently, the parallel redo workers are not working efficiently.
what_to_do: On an older build, patch first; SQL Server Builds lists the current updates. Reduce the bursts: trim index maintenance on the primary and batch large loads. Strengthen the secondary's storage and CPU, since redo writes pages and competes with read queries there. As a tested last resort, trace flag 3459 switches to serial redo; only a restart brings parallel redo back.

title: PARALLEL_REDO_LOG_CACHE Wait Type in SQL Server
verdict: No. The secondary replica redo model write-up lists it among the waits without performance impact, and Get Wait Statistics filters it out by default.

title: PARALLEL_REDO_TRAN_LIST Wait Type in SQL Server

title: PARALLEL_REDO_TRAN_TURN Wait Type in SQL Server
verdict: It can be. Depending on how often inserts happen, it can significantly slow down parallel redo, and its frequency is generally proportional to the volume of inserts.
what_to_do: Reduce page splits at the source: a lower fill factor on the indexes taking random inserts, and index maintenance that keeps them in shape. Give heaps that take updates a clustered index, which removes forwarded records. Re-measure the redo rate on the secondary after the change. Trace flag 3459 switches the instance to serial redo. Once on, only a service restart brings parallel redo back, so treat it as a last resort to test, not a fix.

title: PARALLEL_REDO_WORKER_SYNC Wait Type in SQL Server

title: PREEMPTIVE_DTC Wait Types in SQL Server

For slow calls, test MSDTC between the machines involved. The Test-Dtc PowerShell cmdlet checks the configuration and connectivity, and the MSDTC entries in the Windows event log often name the problem. On a failover cluster or Availability Group, check the DTC setup against the documented guidance for that topology. For Availability Groups that includes the group's DTC_SUPPORT setting.

title: PREEMPTIVE_HADR_LEASE_MECHANISM Wait Type in SQL Server

title: PREEMPTIVE_OLEDBOPS Wait Type in SQL Server

title: PREEMPTIVE_OS Security Wait Types in SQL Server

title: PREEMPTIVE_OS_AUTHENTICATIONOPS Wait Type in SQL Server

Check which domain controller the server uses and whether sites and subnets route it to a nearby one. For accounts in very many groups, cleaning up group membership is the real fix.

title: PREEMPTIVE_OS File Operation Wait Types in SQL Server

title: Miscellaneous PREEMPTIVE_OS Wait Types in SQL Server

title: PREEMPTIVE_OS_CREATEFILE Wait Type in SQL Server

title: PREEMPTIVE_OS Group Lookup Wait Types in SQL Server

Keep group nesting simple for the groups that hold SQL Server logins; every extra level is more work for each lookup.

title: PREEMPTIVE_OS_DSGETDCNAME Wait Type in SQL Server
verdict: At small levels, no; it is not a known contention point, and it was zero on our SQL Server 2025 lab.

verdict: Not in practice; it is not a known contention point.

title: PREEMPTIVE_OS_FLUSHFILEBUFFERS Wait Type in SQL Server
verdict: On Linux, its dominance is expected; on Windows, modest amounts are noise.

title: PREEMPTIVE_OS Library Wait Types in SQL Server

title: PREEMPTIVE_OS_GETDISKFREESPACE Wait Type in SQL Server

title: PREEMPTIVE_OS_GETPROCADDRESS Wait Type in SQL Server
verdict: The lookup itself is quick; our SQL Server 2025 lab had about 3,900 waits totalling half a second in a day.

title: PREEMPTIVE_OS_LOGONUSER Wait Type in SQL Server

title: PREEMPTIVE_OS_LOOKUPACCOUNTSID Wait Type in SQL Server
verdict: Occasional lookups are routine; our SQL Server 2025 lab had about 5,000 waits averaging under a millisecond in a day.
what_to_do: Fix the pattern: translate SIDs once and join or cache the result, instead of calling per row. For audit reports, store the name mappings on a schedule rather than resolving them live. If the average per call is high, give the infrastructure team the numbers; nltest /dsgetdc:YourDomain shows which domain controller the server uses.

title: PREEMPTIVE_OS_PIPEOPS Wait Type in SQL Server
verdict: The wait itself is not; it lasts as long as the external command does.

title: PREEMPTIVE_OS_QUERYREGISTRY Wait Type in SQL Server
verdict: Usually not; on our SQL Server 2025 lab it had about 55,000 waits averaging under a millisecond in a day.
what_to_do: On SQL Server 2022, apply CU5 or later. Otherwise, find the scripts or tools reading the registry and reduce how often they do. If individual registry reads are slow, that points at the operating system, which is a separate investigation.

title: PREEMPTIVE_OS_REPORTEVENT Wait Type in SQL Server
verdict: The call itself is quick when Windows is healthy; our SQL Server 2025 lab had about 4,700 waits totalling 13 seconds in a day.

title: PREEMPTIVE_OS_WAITFORSINGLEOBJECT Wait Type in SQL Server
verdict: Read it the way you read ASYNC_NETWORK_IO: SQL Server has results and is waiting on the client.

title: PREEMPTIVE_OS_WRITEFILEGATHER Wait Type in SQL Server
verdict: Yes, when it shows real duration, because the zeroing happens inside an operation somebody is waiting on.
what_to_do: Turn on instant file initialization by granting the database engine service the Perform volume maintenance tasks right. From SQL Server 2016, setup offers this as a checkbox. It takes effect after a service restart. Pre-size data and log files so growth is rare, and use fixed growth sizes rather than percentages. Keep log growth increments moderate. On SQL Server 2022 and later, a log growth of 64 MB or less can skip zeroing; larger ones cannot. Size tempdb for its normal peak so it does not grow after every restart.

title: PREEMPTIVE_SB_STOPENDPOINT Wait Type in SQL Server
verdict: No. It is not reported as a contention point, and each occurrence is an endpoint stopping rather than workload; our SQL Server 2025 lab had a single wait of a millisecond.

title: PREEMPTIVE_SP_SERVER_DIAGNOSTICS Wait Type in SQL Server
verdict: No. It is not a known contention point; our SQL Server 2025 lab had a single wait.

title: PREEMPTIVE_XE Wait Types in SQL Server

title: PRINT_ROLLBACK_PROGRESS Wait Type in SQL Server
verdict: It measures a deliberate action.

title: PVS_PREALLOCATE Wait Type in SQL Server
verdict: No. It is not a known contention point, and Get Wait Statistics filters it out by default.

title: PWAIT_DIRECTLOGCONSUMER_GETNEXT Wait Type in SQL Server
verdict: No. It is not reported as a contention point; it was zero on our SQL Server 2025 lab.

title: QDS_DYN_VECTOR Wait Type in SQL Server

title: QDS_LOADDB Wait Type in SQL Server
verdict: On SQL Server 2016 and 2017, for systems where failover time matters, it can be: everything looks recovered, but sessions stall while a large Query Store loads.
what_to_do: On SQL Server 2016 and 2017, add trace flag 7752 as a startup flag if failover time matters. On 2019 and later, there is nothing to switch; keep the stores to a sensible size. Right-size each store: a MAX_STORAGE_SIZE_MB that fits your retention needs, and a STALE_QUERY_THRESHOLD_DAYS that trims old history. Smaller stores load faster in any mode.

title: QUERY_EXECUTION_INDEX_SORT_EVENT_OPEN Wait Type in SQL Server
verdict: Not in itself. It follows the length and parallelism of your offline index builds, and it was zero on our SQL Server 2025 lab.

title: QUERY_TASK_ENQUEUE_MUTEX Wait Type in SQL Server

title: RESOURCE_GOVERNOR_IDLE Wait Type in SQL Server
verdict: It is a policy, reported honestly.
what_to_do: Revisit the cap against current intent. If the throttled workload now matters more, raise the cap or move it to a different pool. title: RESOURCE_SEMAPHORE Wait Type in SQL Server

what_to_do: In priority order, and it matches the causes above: fix the query first, the instance second, and reach for a hint or Resource Governor only when you cannot fix either yet. STEP 1

title: RESOURCE_SEMAPHORE_MUTEX Wait Type in SQL Server

title: RESOURCE_SEMAPHORE_QUERY_COMPILE Wait Type in SQL Server
verdict: Short bursts happen after restarts, failovers and deployments, when the plan cache is cold and everything compiles at once.
what_to_do: Find the expensive and repeated compiles. Query Store, or the plan cache with plan_generation_num in sys.dm_exec_query_stats, shows the statements that recompile most. Simplify the worst statements; compile cost grows with complexity, and splitting a giant statement into steps often removes the problem. Improve plan reuse by parameterising ad hoc patterns. Forced parameterization for one database is an option when the application cannot change. Check memory overall. If RESOURCE_SEMAPHORE is high at the same time, the instance is short of memory in general, not just at compile.

title: RESOURCE_SEMAPHORE_SMALL_QUERY Wait Type in SQL Server

what_to_do: Follow the RESOURCE_SEMAPHORE walkthrough: find the queries with the largest grants and fix the reasons for them, such as missing indexes, stale statistics and unnecessary sorts. Check max server memory and overall memory health so grants have room. If you are still on SQL Server 2008 R2 or earlier, the same steps apply, and so does planning the upgrade.

title: RESTORE_MSDA_THREAD_BARRIER Wait Type in SQL Server

title: THREADPOOL Wait Type in SQL Server
verdict: In short bursts, yes.
what_to_do: If it is happening right now, stop the bleeding first: Find the head blocker causing the blocking chain and kill it: KILL [session_id]; -- the head blocker session This releases all blocked sessions, which release their threads. Do not kill random sessions, find the head blocker first. If new connections are failing, connect with the dedicated administrator connection (DAC) to find and kill it; Microsoft's max worker threads page gives the same advice. If it is not a blocking problem but a load problem: identify the application sending the most concurrent requests and throttle it at the connection pool level while you investigate. Fix the underlying causes: For blocking-driven THREADPOOL: Investigate and fix the blocking root cause (see LCK_M_X post) If the blocked sessions are readers waiting on writers ( LCK_M_S behind an LCK_M_X ), read committed snapshot isolation (RCSI) can remove that conflict. It has a cost: row versions are kept in tempdb's version store, and readers get the last committed version instead of waiting, which changes what the application reads. title: TRACEWRITE Wait Type in SQL Server
verdict: Yes, when it is significant.
what_to_do: Stop or narrow the rowset trace: sp_trace_setstatus stops a trace by its id; if tracing must continue, capture fewer events with tighter filters, to a local file rather than live. Move to Extended Events; SQL Trace is deprecated, and Extended Events is the replacement. Check sys.traces as part of routine health checks so abandoned traces do not linger.

title: WAIT_ON_SYNC_STATISTICS_REFRESH Wait Type in SQL Server
verdict: It is when it shows real duration, because a user query is paying for statistics maintenance at a random moment.
what_to_do: Turn on asynchronous statistics updates for the database: ALTER DATABASE [YourDb] SET AUTO_UPDATE_STATISTICS_ASYNC ON;. Queries then compile with the existing statistics while the update runs in the background, so they never wait for it. The trade is that a query may run once more on stale statistics. On SQL Server 2022 and later, also consider the ASYNC_STATS_UPDATE_WAIT_AT_LOW_PRIORITY database scoped configuration, for the case where the background update's schema modification lock gets in the way of other queries. Update statistics yourself on the tables that churn, straight after their load windows, so automatic updates rarely need to fire during the day. Avoid FULLSCAN on very large tables unless a plan needs it.

title: WAIT_XTP_CKPT_CLOSE Wait Type in SQL Server

title: WAIT_XTP_RECOVERY Wait Type in SQL Server
verdict: The wait is honest; its duration is the operational fact.

title: WAIT_XTP_TASK_SHUTDOWN Wait Type in SQL Server

title: WRITELOG Wait Type in SQL Server
verdict: Yes, some WRITELOG is inherent in any transactional workload.
when_to_ignore: High transaction volume workloads, if you are doing tens of thousands of commits per second, some WRITELOG is unavoidable.
what_to_do: Slow log disk: Move the log file to a dedicated fast disk (SSD or NVMe ideally) Separate log files from data files if they share a volume Check storage queue depth in Performance Monitor ( PhysicalDisk\Current Disk Queue Length on the log volume) Chatty commit patterns: Identify the application or job doing frequent small commits Refactor row-by-row inserts into set-based operations Or batch commits, instead of committing after every row, commit every 500 or 1000 rows Review SSIS or ETL packages for Row by Row commit modes AG secondary lag: this is a HADR_SYNC_COMMIT problem rather than a WRITELOG one. The HADR_SYNC_COMMIT page covers the network, the secondary's log disk and when asynchronous commit fits. As a temporary measure only: For write-heavy applications under strict SLA, delayed durability ( DELAYED_DURABILITY = FORCED ) can reduce WRITELOG by batching log flushes. This trades durability for speed: the commit returns before its log records are on disk, so a crash or a restart can lose the most recent committed transactions. Appropriate only for specific use cases (audit logs, telemetry) not for transactional data.

title: WRITE_COMPLETION Wait Type in SQL Server
verdict: A small baseline is normal; our SQL Server 2025 lab had about 1,850 waits averaging half a millisecond in a day.
what_to_do: If integrity checks drive it, run them off-peak, or on a restored copy on another server, which also tests your backups. If user snapshots drive it, keep fewer of them for less time. If file growth drives it, pre-size files so growth is rare. If writes are slow across the board, take the per-file latency to the storage team.
